title: NGC 7232/3
caption: The interacting galaxy trio LGG 455 (NGC 7232, NGC 7233 and NGC 7232B), imaged by Gemini South
credit: International Gemini Observatory/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA/T. A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage)

recognition.text: Published in the NSF NOIRLab image archive. No published rating.

story: Three galaxies share this view, with NGC 7232 at upper right, NGC 7233 at lower right and NGC 7232B on the left. Together they form an interacting trio called Lyon Group of Galaxies #455, or LGG 455. The two brightest points near the centre are not galaxies at all, but foreground stars in our own Milky Way.
Dark lanes of dust cross NGC 7232 and NGC 7233, while NGC 7232B has bright spots of young, blue stars scattered along its weak spiral arms.

Little detailed research has been done on the group, but it is thought to contain a rare 'dark galaxy', a cloud holding the raw ingredients for stars that has never managed to form any. Its gas could make more than 400 million Suns, yet deep Gemini imaging finds no significant population of stars there, just left of the lower foreground star.

understand.summary: The data were taken with the Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph (GMOS) on Gemini South in Chile, in visible and near-infrared light through g, r and i filters. The source does not say which colour each filter was assigned.
understand.eye: These galaxies are far too faint for the eye. A large telescope collecting light over long exposures reveals their dust lanes and young stars.

explore: Most likely, that gas was thrown out of NGC 7233 when it passed close to one of the other two galaxies. Ryan Soares suggested this field for the Australian/Gemini Student Imaging Contest, and Travis Rector of the University of Alaska Anchorage produced the colour composite.
alt: Two galaxies with dark dust lanes on the right and a spiral with blue spots on the left, with two bright foreground stars near the centre.
